hero.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI rules for courtrooms after rampant misuse
hero.body:
Florida attorneys and self-represented litigants must soon verify that everything they cite in court actually exists and is accurate. The Florida Supreme Court has adopted new rules to combat a growing crisis of artificial intelligence misuse in courtrooms, with the regulations taking effect June 15. The problem of fake evidence, fabricated facts, and bogus case law has become so widespread that the state's highest court felt compelled to take action. Those who violate the rules face consequences ranging from public reprimand to fines and suspension.

Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has worked to control AI use in courts after witnessing its misuse firsthand in his own courtroom. Matthewman said, "It's really a problem," and expressed concern that the situation will worsen before improving. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better. I think the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, but I unfortunately have seen over the last couple of years that it is growing and growing and growing," he said. Criminal defense attorney Paul Figueroa in Tampa, who recently began using AI to improve his work, emphasized that the technology is unreliable. "It can be something as simple as it gives a quote that's directly on point to my case, and you go, all right, this is brilliant, this is what I've been looking for, I could have searched 300 cases and not come up with anything better than this, and then you realize that's not in the case," Figueroa explained. When asked whether the new rules are sufficient, Figueroa responded, "I do. I think it goes far enough for what we know now."

A recent case in Polk County illustrates the severity of the problem. An attorney representing the Polk County School District in a lawsuit over school bus cameras was publicly criticized after a judge found fabricated facts and nonexistent case citations in a motion to dismiss. The attorney acknowledged using ChatGPT as a drafting and research tool but stated, "there was no excuse" for his "failure to verify…before filing." The school district said it takes accuracy and integrity in legal proceedings seriously and is evaluating whether to continue using the attorney's services.

Matthewman issued a warning to all legal professionals and self-represented parties. "I would caution lawyers and parties representing themselves to make sure everything you file in court is accurate, because if not, you could find yourself in hot water," he said. The Florida Supreme Court's order represents an important step in addressing AI-related problems in the justice system, though concerns remain about whether it will be enough to stem the tide of technology misuse in courtrooms.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island official warns town 'reapplying Band-Aid' as erosion threatens to split island at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A new Florida Department of Environmental Protection report found Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report reveals that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile coastline faces severe erosion that could breach the island at Peck Lake, potentially splitting it in half. The threat stretches across the entire barrier island, from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where ocean water could transform a thin strip of land into an open inlet. This scenario has occurred before. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s until the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back with sand. The current erosion crisis jeopardizes not only roads, buildings, and drainage systems but also natural habitats, wildlife, and ancient archaeological sites that characterize the island.

The environmental threat extends beyond physical infrastructure. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society cautioned that future storm surges could create additional breaches, making coastal marshes and other ecosystems vulnerable. He emphasized that over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these conservation areas, along with historical and prehistorical sites at risk. The Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, has already lost half its mass to erosion. Wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park face similar threats. A second state assessment warned that mangrove swamps critical for habitat and coastal protection are also threatened by erosion, while rising water levels could displace entire species on the island.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field acknowledged the severity of the situation, describing the town's current approach as temporary at best. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. The town completed a major beach renourishment project in April 2025, depositing enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field noted that no oceanfront homes face immediate danger only because of this continuous maintenance effort. However, the island spent approximately three million dollars in taxpayer funds annually on beach renourishment, a financial commitment that cannot be sustained indefinitely.

Field warned that without guaranteed funding sources, Jupiter Island faces a precarious future. If the island were to breach, repairs could require substantial state and federal investment. "We would have cataclysmic erosion if we didn't get federal funding and state funding," Field said. He added that if beach renourishment funding disappeared, Florida's coastline would transform rapidly in undesirable ways. Field suggested the recent FDEP assessment strengthens Jupiter Island's position to compete for state and federal grants to address erosion. As sea levels continue rising faster than historical rates, the long-term viability of the island depends on securing sustained financial support for protection measures.

cards.headline: Florida fireworks ban under consideration for Fourth of July's 250th anniversary due to statewide drought
cards.body:
Florida's Independence Day celebrations this year could be significantly affected by severe drought conditions sweeping across the state. State leaders are currently evaluating whether to implement a statewide fireworks ban for the Fourth of July's 250th anniversary celebration. According to the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, the current drought conditions are even more severe than those experienced in 1998, when Florida last enacted a statewide fireworks ban. Every region of Florida is experiencing at least abnormally dry conditions, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast facing particularly serious moderate to extreme drought situations.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson warned about the potential ban as early as May, emphasizing the serious fire hazard that fireworks could pose during these conditions. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said. While acknowledging the historical importance of the 250th anniversary celebration, Simpson urged residents to begin considering alternative ways to mark the occasion. The Department of Agriculture has indicated that implementing a fireworks ban would be considered a last resort measure rather than the preferred approach.

Despite the potential restrictions on the horizon, fireworks retailers are experiencing a surge in customer activity ahead of the holiday. Bill Murphy, manager at Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, reported increased foot traffic as customers shop early in anticipation of potential regulations. The store takes drought conditions seriously and closely monitors the drought index to assess whether soil moisture levels are adequate for safe fireworks use. Murphy expressed cautious optimism about the situation, noting that weather forecasts predict significant rainfall in the coming weeks that could alleviate current dry conditions.

State officials have not yet made a final decision regarding the fireworks ban and will continue monitoring drought conditions closely through the Fourth of July. The balance between public safety and the desire to celebrate a historic milestone remains at the center of this discussion. Leaders are carefully weighing fire risk concerns against the public's expectations for traditional Independence Day festivities. Residents and fireworks businesses alike are watching the weather forecasts and drought updates as the decision date approaches, hoping that adequate rainfall will make the ban unnecessary.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County residents are banned from using fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns and landscaping to reduce nutrient runoff during rainy season.
cards.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties are prohibited from using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The restriction is designed to address environmental concerns during Florida's rainy season, when nutrient-rich runoff can trigger algae blooms in local waterways. According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, reducing these nutrients in runoff is essential to protecting the region's aquatic ecosystems.

The algae blooms that result from excess nutrients pose serious threats to the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River. Skaggs explained that these blooms can have multiple harmful effects on the local environment. They shade out the beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In some cases, when algae blooms reach certain densities, they can release toxins into the water. These toxins can damage human health, harm wildlife populations, and degrade the overall health of the ecosystem.

Residents looking for alternatives during the ban period have options that can be equally effective. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical solution for gardens and landscaping. Composting provides nutrients to your landscape and can be implemented in simple ways. Ricketts described a small composting container as an easy and practical approach that accomplishes the goal of adding nutrients naturally to your outdoor spaces without relying on chemical fertilizers.

The ban affects anyone maintaining lawns or landscaping in these three counties and will remain in effect during the months when rainfall increases nutrient runoff into local waterways. By switching to composting and other organic methods, property owners can maintain their gardens and landscapes while supporting the environmental goals behind the restriction.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after home security camera catches burglary in real time
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie resident watching his home security camera remotely activated an audible siren when he spotted a masked man inside his apartment at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes on Thursday afternoon.
cards.body:
Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following an incident Thursday afternoon at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail. Around 3:38 p.m., the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. Upon checking his live camera feed, he spotted a masked man inside his apartment. The resident activated his camera's audible siren, which caused the suspect to leave briefly, but the man returned and tampered with the camera.

Multiple witnesses observed the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. Port St. Lucie Police arrived and discovered clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River counties could lose millions under Florida property tax proposal on November ballot

cards.body:
Government officials across the Treasure Coast are assessing the impact of a property tax reform referendum scheduled for November that would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to a Florida Association of Counties study, Martin County could lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29, St. Lucie County could lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29, and Indian River County could lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Local officials are restricted by the state from speaking out against or endorsing the referendum but can provide educational information about it.

If the measure passes, local governments are considering options including finding new revenue sources or making budget cuts. Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell noted that potential solutions could involve increasing sales tax or user fees for services, though no decisions have been made. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, supports the proposal, saying it targets struggling families in $300,000 homes. Republican lawmakers, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, contend local governments are taking in too much tax revenue and spending too much. Homeowner savings will vary from hundreds to thousands of dollars depending on the county, city, and assessed home value.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs

cards.body:
An Okeechobee County woman is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after claiming she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs they purchased in June 2024. Mary Hubbard bought the product at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the lawsuit, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. The lawsuit seeks $50,000 in damages and alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Stuart-based dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban they say threatens conservation businesses
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing criticism from shark diving operators, including Nathan Campbell, owner of Stuart-based Emerald Charters.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, H.R. 3831, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. A coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible encounters with sharks, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators have not been given the opportunity to present data to Congress. Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, arguing this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent, but Florida operators point to different outcomes. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Since Hawaii's ban, operators note that shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. Campbell has urged senators to delay action and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island faces threat of split as erosion reaches critical levels
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that erosion along Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has become so severe the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater to survive, making coastal marshes vulnerable. Among the sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry noted there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project. Field said no oceanfront homes are in immediate danger but only because of ongoing work. He described the town as "reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over" and said the island would face "cataclysmic erosion" without federal and state funding. About $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment annually.

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup and Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs after eating them and developed parasitic infections and other medical complications.

Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County filed a lawsuit against Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in their SpaghettiOs. According to the complaint, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food product. She documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food. The incident occurred in June 2024 when Hubbard purchased the SpaghettiOs at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.

Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications following the incident. The lawsuit alleges the companies failed to properly inspect the product and seeks $50,000 in damages. Campbell Soup Co. said the claims lack merit, while Walmart stated it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators oppose federal feeding ban targeting waters off state coast

cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry. The measure, H.R. 3831, also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education and conservation, while leaving fishing practices untouched.

Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators are requesting the chance to speak and share the science and facts. He noted that no one from Congress has yet asked them to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members point to Hawaii's 2006 ban, noting that since the ban, shark incidents have increased and fatalities have been reported. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping new rules.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program overwhelmed with 8,000 monthly calls for help
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County's Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in grant funding for emergency rental assistance, but demand far outweighs the funds available each month.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program is overwhelmed by demand, receiving nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month. The Community Services Department has nearly $2 million in combined grant funding for the program, but applications fill rapidly when they open at the beginning of each month. Currently, about 800 applications are in the queue, with typically about 600 submitted within the first couple of hours of opening. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked CLOSED due to high demand. Program director Dr. James Green said: "We're doing what we can to prioritize and serve those who are most needy but the demand it far outweighs the resources that are available." According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month.

Green urges anyone needing assistance to call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability. For those unable to access the county program, 211 is available 24/7 and connects residents with nonprofits and other assistance programs in the area. Green said the recent surge in applications is partly due to rising costs of living, including housing, gas, and food. He emphasized the importance of keeping residents in their homes so they can continue to work and support their families.

The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November and requires 60% approval to pass. In Palm Beach County, over half of properties have the homestead exemption, higher than the state average of 47%.

More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean on June 13 in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis event. Participants launch from Bimini, Bahamas at midnight and are expected to arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. Event founder Travis Suit established the fundraiser to benefit the Pipers Angels Foundation, which he created in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, while crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong beach celebration marking the paddlers' arrival. He argued the stadium should be funded through user fees and tourism tax dollars alone. Wostal reiterated his concerns that the county has not received detailed site plans, proof of financing or documentation supporting the team's claimed $2.3 billion project cost. He questioned economic assumptions being used to promote the deal, citing an outside review that found the Rays cast doubt on projections the development would generate $6 billion in tax revenue over 35 years. hero.headline: Jupiter Island erosion could split island in half at Peck Lake, state report warns
hero.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report has sounded an alarm about severe erosion along Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile coastline. The damage threatens infrastructure like roads and buildings as well as the natural ecosystems and historical sites that characterize this barrier island. Most dramatically, the erosion has become so critical that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially dividing the island in two. This threat extends across the island's length, from Blowing Rocks Preserve where private development already faces risk to Peck Lake, where a breach would transform a narrow strip of land into an open inlet. History shows this is not merely theoretical. A storm created such a breach at Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers refilled the opening with sand.

The ecological consequences of a future breach would be severe. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society explained that ecosystems in the area depend on maintaining a careful balance between fresh and saltwater. Another breach could destabilize these systems and coastal marshes. Perry noted that more intense storm surges in the future could create additional breaks in the shoreline. Beyond the immediate coastline, over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these conservation areas. At particular risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site between 3,000 and 4,000 years old that has already lost half its area to erosion. Wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park also face danger. A second state assessment warned that mangrove swamps essential for habitat and coastal protection are eroding, while rising water levels could displace entire species from the island.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field acknowledged that sea level rise is a documented reality, having accelerated particularly over the last 15 years. He said the town fights erosion through constant maintenance efforts. In April 2025, Jupiter Island completed a major beach renourishment project adding enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field stated that no oceanfront homes face immediate danger, but only because of these ongoing interventions. He described the approach candidly as "just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," something the town will continue as long as funding exists.

The town currently spends approximately $3 million annually from taxpayer dollars on beach renourishment. Field warned that if the island experiences a breach, repairs would require substantial state and federal investment. He cautioned that if beach renourishment funding ever stops, Florida's coastline could change rapidly and unpredictably. The recent FDEP assessment should strengthen Jupiter Island's position in competing for state and federal mitigation funding.

hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties are prohibited from using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. Composting provides nutrients to your landscape and can be implemented in simple ways. Ricketts described a small composting container as an easy and practical approach that accomplishes the goal of adding nutrients naturally to your outdoor spaces without relying on chemical fertilizers.

The ban affects anyone maintaining lawns or landscaping in these three counties and will remain in effect during the months when rainfall increases nutrient runoff into local waterways. By switching to composting and other organic methods, property owners can maintain their gardens and landscapes while supporting the environmental goals behind the restriction.
